title: Early Emphysema and a Brother With Cirrhosis / Test the Family, Stop the Smoking First

blocks.text: Early Emphysema and a Brother With Cirrhosis / Test the Family, Stop the Smoking First

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-33 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) · Guidelines: European Respiratory Society statement: diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary disease in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (Eur Respir J 2017;50:1700610); NICE technology appraisal TA965 Human alpha1-proteinase inhibitor for treating emphysema (terminated appraisal, 2024) · Related AMaC: AMaC COPD station; this one tests the genetic cause of early emphysema

Dear Doctor, a 44-year-old electrician. He is breathless on hills and has a morning cough. A CT scan shows emphysema at the lung bases. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day. His brother has cirrhosis. Please assess and advise.
The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Emphysema at the bases at 44, with a brother who has cirrhosis, is alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency until tested. The station turns on the right test, the family testing and the fact that smoking must stop first.

The Examiner Trap. He hopes a drug will fix his lungs so that he can carry on smoking. Candidates promise an infusion, or label him as COPD. Pass: level then genotype, smoking cessation first, liver check, family testing. Fail: treat as ordinary COPD.

Say
Do
Ask about breathlessness, cough, smoking, alcohol, liver problems and his family's lung and liver history.
"How far can you walk? How much do you smoke and drink? Has anyone in the family had lung or liver disease?"
Breathlessness; cough; smoking; alcohol; jaundice; brother; parents; children; work; vaccines.
Examine the chest, look for liver disease and check his oxygen levels.
"May I listen to your chest, check your oxygen and examine your tummy? Tell me if anything hurts."
Oxygen; chest shape; breath sounds; clubbing; jaundice; spider naevi; liver; spleen; cover him.
Explain what you suspect, the blood test and what it means for his family, and why smoking must stop.
"I think an inherited protein shortage is damaging your lungs. A blood test will tell us. Your family may need testing."
Level; genotype; liver tests; smoking; alcohol; vaccines; family; follow-up; augmentation is not routinely available (NICE TA965).

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 44-year-old electrician. You are blunt, worried and a little defensive about smoking.
Opening line: "I'm not old enough to have emphysema. It's just a smoker's cough."
Volunteered: you smoke 15 a day and have done since you were 17.
Only if asked: you drink about 14 pints a week. Your brother has cirrhosis and your father died of lung disease at 55. You have two children, 14 and 11.

Only if asked about jaundice or swelling: none. You have had chest infections most winters. You use a blue inhaler now and then and take no other regular medicines; no allergies. As an electrician you have worked around some dust and fumes but no asbestos that you know of. No recent travel. You live with your wife and children.
Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid your children have it. Say: "If I've given my kids this, I'll never forgive myself."
Your questions, in your own words: "Is it genetic?" "Can you give me a drip to fix it?" "Do I have to stop smoking?"
How you react: if lectured, you bristle. If listened to and offered support, you engage. If offered options, you choose.

Findings, released when examined: breathless on stairs; respiratory rate 18; pulse 80 regular; blood pressure 126/78; SpO2 94% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. Hyperinflated chest. Quiet breath sounds at the bases. No clubbing. No jaundice. Abdomen soft, no hepatomegaly.
Results, only when requested: alpha-1 antitrypsin level low; genotype ZZ. Liver tests: raised transaminases. Liver ultrasound: coarse texture. Lung function: obstruction with reduced gas transfer.

Question ladder: 1. Who should be tested for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency? (D) 2. How is it tested? (E) 3. Is augmentation available on the NHS? (E) NICE could not make a recommendation (TA965 terminated) because the manufacturer does not intend to launch it in England and Wales, mainly because it could not offer a price that meets the cost-effectiveness threshold; any access is a specialist and local commissioning enquiry. 4. Does augmentation help the liver? (E) 5. Which lifestyle advice matters? (E)

Curveballs: He asks for the infusion now and to keep smoking: smoking cessation comes first, there is no benefit shown in current smokers (ERS 2017), and NICE made no recommendation on augmentation (TA965 terminated); any access is a specialist and local commissioning enquiry. He asks about his children: if he is ZZ each child carries at least one Z gene; testing children is discussed with the specialist or genetics team, all of them should avoid smoking, and his brother should be offered testing. He asks about alcohol: avoid it with liver disease.

Suspects alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in early basal emphysema (D)
Requests the level, then genotype or phenotype (E)
Says smoking cessation comes first and that NICE made no recommendation on augmentation (TA965 terminated), which would not treat liver disease (E)
Says augmentation does not help liver disease (E)

CANDIDATE: Lift your shirt. [R1 Fail] Do you smoke? [R2 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Skips the abdomen.) [R3 Fail] Ordinary COPD. [R4 Fail] Another chest X-ray. [R5 Fail]
CANDIDATE: I'll start the infusion and you can carry on smoking. [R6 Fail] Nothing to worry about. [R7 Fail] See your GP. [R8 Fail]
Examiner note: No consent, the abdomen skipped, a genetic cause missed, and an infusion promised to a man who keeps smoking.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I listen to your chest, check your oxygen and examine your tummy? Tell me if anything hurts. I'll cover you afterwards. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: How breathless are you, and do you cough? Any yellowing of the skin? How much do you drink? Has anyone in the family had lung or liver disease? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: About 14 pints. My brother has cirrhosis. My dad died of lung disease.
CANDIDATE: (Examines, then covers him.) A hyperinflated chest, quiet basal breath sounds, and a normal abdomen. Thank you for letting me examine you. [R3 Pass] [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: I suspect an inherited condition called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, as well as the smoking. [R4 Pass]
CANDIDATE: A blood level first, then a genotype, plus liver tests and an ultrasound. [R5 Pass]

CANDIDATE: Stopping smoking is the most important thing you can do for your lungs. NICE has not been able to assess the drip you asked about because the company is not launching it here, so it is not routinely available, and the specialist team would only look at access as a special request; there is no evidence it helps while you smoke, and it would not treat your liver. Cut right back on alcohol, and I will make sure your vaccines are up to date. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What worries you most? [R7 Pass]
PATIENT: My kids having it.

CANDIDATE: That is a fair fear. If the test shows two copies, each of your children carries at least one; we would talk to the specialist team about testing them and keeping them away from cigarettes, and offer your brother a test. [R7 Pass] Shall we do the blood test now? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Suspected the genetic cause, put smoking first and planned family testing. Did not name linked conditions, vaccines, transplant or a written plan.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? This could be a shock. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any dust at work? Are your vaccinations up to date? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) No clubbing, jaundice or liver stigmata, and oxygen saturation 94%. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: It is a laboratory diagnosis; bronchiectasis and liver disease are linked. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: The level alone misses carriers, so we'll add the genotype and lung function. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: Inhalers and pulmonary rehabilitation help now; transplant assessment is considered if the lung disease becomes severe; vaccines protect you. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: We'll plan how to talk to your children. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll give you a written plan and an annual review. [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone, occupational dust, vaccines, linked conditions, carrier testing, transplant and a written plan.
R2: Not asking about his brother's cirrhosis. It points to a genetic cause.
R4: Calling it ordinary COPD. Emphysema at the bases at 44 with liver disease in the family needs a genetic test.
R5: Relying on the level alone. It misses carriers; a genotype or phenotype is needed.
R6: Promising an infusion to a smoker. Smoking cessation comes first, and NICE made no recommendation on augmentation (TA965 terminated), so it is not routinely available.
"Can I ask about liver or lung disease in your family?"
"Emphysema this early makes me think of an inherited cause."
"I'd like to check I've understood what worries you most."

ERS statement (Eur Respir J 2017;50:1700610): test everyone with COPD or adult-onset asthma; targeted testing applies to early-onset COPD, basal panlobular emphysema and a family history of COPD or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency; unexplained cirrhosis also raises suspicion. Testing of relatives, starting with siblings, should be considered after counselling and with consent.

Measure the serum level first, then confirm with phenotype or genotype; the level alone misses heterozygotes. Ensure smoking has stopped. Weekly intravenous augmentation slowed emphysema progression on CT in trials, with no evidence of benefit in current smokers or in SZ and MZ carriers, and it does not treat liver disease (ERS 2017). NICE could not make a recommendation on Respreeza (TA965, appraisal terminated 2024) because the company said it does not intend to launch it in England and Wales; there is therefore no NICE guidance to support routine commissioning. This is an access statement, not a judgement on efficacy or licensing; any individual request goes through the specialist centre and local commissioner.

Advice: avoid smoke and occupational exposures, treat infections promptly, limit alcohol (none if liver disease), vaccinate against influenza, pneumonia and hepatitis, annual lung and liver monitoring.
THINK: Early basal emphysema, family liver disease: alpha-1.
SAY: "An inherited protein shortage may be damaging your lungs."
DO: Ask family liver and lung history; examine the abdomen.
NUMBERS: Level first, then genotype (ERS 2017); no NICE recommendation for augmentation (TA965 terminated, 2024); access is a specialist and local commissioning enquiry.
TRAP: Ordinary COPD; promising an infusion.
FINISH: Level, genotype, liver tests, stop smoking, family.

Eur Respir J 2017;50:1700610. https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.00610-2017 Supports: who to test, testing sequence, family testing, smoking, augmentation evidence and lung transplantation.

Human alpha1-proteinase inhibitor for treating emphysema (terminated appraisal), TA965, terminated 2024. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/terminated/ta965 Supports: NICE could not recommend augmentation; the company does not intend to launch it in England and Wales, so there is no NICE guidance to support commissioning. Access is a specialist and local commissioning enquiry.
